title: The AI bugpocalypse is here. Now what? - Jack Cable, Corridor
talk_summary: Jack Cable argues that AI coding agents are introducing vulnerabilities at scale (20-40% of the time per Backsbench), but that most exploited vulnerability classes are old and preventable by design, not by one-off patching. He recommends shifting to systemic controls — memory-safe languages, guardrails before the PR, and AI-assisted review — rather than whack-a-mole fixes.

takeaways.technique: Pre-PR guardrails instead of post-hoc review
takeaways.what_they_do: Corridor positions security tooling to catch issues before the pull request is opened, so security isn't a merge blocker and acceleration still wins.
takeaways.evidence_quote: our perspective at Corridor is around preventing vulnerabilities before the pull request

takeaways.technique: Target recurring vulnerability classes, not novel bugs
takeaways.what_they_do: They note nearly all model-found vulns are known classes (buffer overflows, authz bugs), so controls can be class-based and reusable rather than per-instance.
takeaways.evidence_quote: pretty much all of the vulnerabilities that even frontier AI models are finding aren't anything new
takeaways.numbers: 60-70% of vulns in memory-unsafe languages preventable via memory-safe languages

takeaways.what_they_do: They observe that remaining AI-introduced bugs are increasingly contextual (authorization, business logic) that models lack proprietary context to catch.
takeaways.evidence_quote: more so contextual issues. Right? Things like authorization bugs that require an in-depth understanding of a company's business logic
takeaways.numbers: Backsbench: best models introduce vulns 20-40% of the time

takeaways.what_they_do: Argues for one-time structural fixes (e.g., memory-safe rewrites) that pay dividends against future smarter models, versus repeated patching.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we could pour millions of dollars into essentially playing whack-a-mole with vulnerabilities
takeaways.numbers: Android memory-safety vuln share fell ~75% (2019) to ~30% (2022) by writing new code in memory-safe languages

takeaways.what_they_do: They argue AI code review will become the majority, but only viable if tooling gives assurance so humans can reduce oversight.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the majority of code that is being shipped will be reviewed uh not by human but by AI
